title: What I Learned from Studying Abroad
paragraphs: In this study abroad, after training for a total of 9 weeks, 4.5 weeks in medical oncology and 4.5 weeks in endocrinology, at Johns Hopkins University Hospital in Baltimore, America, I was allowed to observe ophthalmology as an observer for three weeks at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary, a hospital affiliated with Harvard University in Boston. I now recall with nostalgia boarding the plane to America in late March this year, feeling various anxieties. I am truly grateful to the doctors of the International Collaboration Office of the Nagoya University School of Medicine who supported this study abroad, the doctors who taught me locally, the host family who hosted me locally, my family, and the scholarship program, Tobitate! Study Abroad JAPAN. Thank you.

The first department I rotated through was medical oncology. For the first three weeks I rotated on the solid tumor team, and then for a week and a half on the leukemia team. The clerkship in medical oncology centred on the ward; I was always in charge of about two patients, checked the data and charts every day, examined the patients, and gave presentations at the attending rounds. In a word, medical oncology was a harrowing ward, with many patients in a very serious condition. One of the patients I was in charge of was receiving chemotherapy for advanced esophageal cancer, but intense nausea from cisplatin occurred, and on some days he vomited 20 to 30 times in one night. Also, a patient who developed chronic pancreatitis as a side effect of the PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab had opioid analgesics work poorly and had intense pain of 10 on a scale of 10 for many days.

The second department was endocrinology. In the morning outpatient clinic, I examined the patient before the attending's main examination and gave a presentation to the attending in front of the patient. Examining first-visit patients and writing charts was difficult: I had to judge the important information in the faxes that had been sent, summarise it in chronological order, and combine it with what the patient said to write in the chart. Every day I checked the chart of each patient coming to the clinic of the attending in charge of me and prepared by finding out what disease and course each patient had. Even so, there were times when I could take histories and do physical examinations relatively well, and times when I could not draw out the information well or could not summarise the history. Also, in the afternoon consult service, for consults from other departments I examined the patients together with the fellow, helped write the consult note, and sometimes presented in front of the attending. The consult cases I was allowed to do included follow-up after pituitary surgery, hypercalcemia, and management of adrenal insufficiency due to a side effect of a PD-1 inhibitor. When writing consult notes, I felt my shortcomings not only in my medical knowledge but also in the ability to write long passages in English in a short time, that is, writing skill. The attending's remarks when I or the fellow presented on a consult were extremely to the point, based on a great deal of evidence, and were helpful.

For the last three weeks, I was allowed to observe as an ophthalmology observer at the Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary, a Harvard University-affiliated hospital. Within ophthalmology I was assigned to the retina group, and in the outpatient clinic I was allowed to see various cases such as age-related macular degeneration, retinal detachment, Von Hippel-Lindau disease, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease and retinopathy of prematurity. I also observed vitrectomy and scleral buckling. At the Harvard Ophthalmology Annual Meeting held once a year, I was able to hear very exciting lectures on the latest surgical methods, gene therapy for retinitis pigmentosa, and artificial retinas.

During the rotations I felt several differences between America and Japan. The first is that the division of labour among occupations is advanced in America. A social worker always accompanied rounds and discussed with the doctors to which rehabilitation facility or hospice to move the patient. There is also a qualification called nurse practitioner, and although they do not have a medical license, they performed bone marrow biopsies. The doctor's job is to examine patients, grasp the information, and order procedures and tests, and actual line placement and drug administration were done by nurses. With such a system, in America even clinicians can devote time to research and private life.

The second is the high frequency of use of painkillers. In particular, the strong opioid oxycodone was used very often, and it was used even for a patient with joint pain suspected to be gout. Also, in bone marrow aspiration and biopsy there were many occasions when the opioid fentanyl was used, not only the local anesthetic lidocaine.

The third difference is about patients. Of course there are various patients in both Japan and America, but as a general tendency I feel that Japanese patients are relatively compliant and many leave the choice of treatment to the doctor. In examinations in the medical oncology clinic, there were many occasions when the patient's family had researched various treatments and asked the doctor how about this treatment. Some patients also brought a list of clinical trials currently being conducted. On the other hand, there were also many patients who complained strongly of pain, and there were often occasions when opioid analgesics were used where in Japan lidocaine alone would have sufficed.

The fourth is about wards and outpatient clinics. First, regarding the ward, my impression was that in America the length of stay on the ward is very short and patients are discharged immediately once stable. On rounds too, every day they talked with the patient about when discharge might be possible, and the social worker discussed with the patient to which rehabilitation facility or hospice they would go. There was also a service called IPOP in which bone marrow transplantation is done on an outpatient basis. On the other hand, in the outpatient clinic, conversely, the American medical oncology clinic often spent more than an hour on one patient. In endocrinology too, since students and residents examine first, the total time spent per patient was longer than in Japan.

Furthermore, a difference in the educational system for doctors can be mentioned. In America, after graduating from medical school, education for doctors is carried out along programs called residency and fellowship. Each program has a different person in charge even in the same department of the same hospital, and the content of the program receives regular evaluation by third-party bodies, so quality is maintained. Also, so that residents and fellows can receive appropriate education, attendings actively let them experience cases. In Japan there is no unified program, so the content and quality of postgraduate training differ from hospital to hospital.

And as for doing research in America, there are several merits. One is that facilities are cheap and various devices can be obtained more cheaply than in Japan, and the second is that there is a lot of collaboration with other fields. In particular, some doctors said it is a waste that there is little collaboration in Japan because Japanese engineering is at the top level in the world. Furthermore, donations are very numerous, as with a chair of research, and the amount of funds available for research seems large.

Finally, this study abroad was one of the biggest events in my life when I look back. There were many things I could realise only by seeing the place with my own eyes during the study abroad, and much information I gained, and they were very helpful in thinking about my future. Also, before going I had the image that America is more advanced, but having actually gone, I felt the high level of Japanese medical care and the diligence and high morals of the Japanese, and came to be proud of myself for having been born Japanese and raised with a Japanese education. As for my future, besides doing clinical work and research in my own specialty, I hope I can do work to improve the Japanese system and to spread the wonderful aspects of Japanese medical care to the world.
Now, I would like to thank everyone who supported my study abroad. Thank you.
